objectives: Distinguish GDP, GNI, NDP; nominal vs real.
Apply the income + expenditure + production approaches.

slides.title: GDP, GNI, NDP: measuring an economy
slides.body:
**Macroeconomics** studies aggregate behavior: total output, employment, inflation, growth. Foundation built ~1930s-40s (Keynes + Kuznets) with national-income accounting.

**GDP (Gross Domestic Product)**: market value of all final goods + services produced within a country in a period (typically year or quarter).

Three equivalent computations:
• **Production approach**: sum of value added by all firms. GDP = ∑ (output − intermediate inputs).
• **Expenditure approach**: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), where C=consumption, I=investment, G=government spending, X=exports, M=imports.
• **Income approach**: GDP = wages + profits + rents + interest + indirect taxes.

All three approaches yield the same GDP (definitionally, with some statistical discrepancy in practice).

**Related measures**:
- **GNI (Gross National Income)**: GDP + net foreign income (from abroad − to abroad). Used by IMF + World Bank.
- **NDP (Net Domestic Product)**: GDP − depreciation of capital.
- **NNP (Net National Product)**: GNI − depreciation.
- **NI (National Income)**: NNP − indirect taxes.
- **Personal Income (PI)**, **Disposable Income (DI)**: household measures.

**Nominal vs Real**:
- **Nominal GDP**: in current prices.
- **Real GDP**: in constant prices (deflated by price index). Removes inflation; comparable over time.
- **GDP deflator**: price index implicit in real GDP calculation. Nominal/Real × 100.
- **CPI (Consumer Price Index)**: another price index; weighted basket of household goods. CPI ≠ GDP deflator (CPI doesn't include investment goods + exports; deflator covers all GDP).

**GDP growth rate**: % change in real GDP. Trend ~2% / yr for developed economies; varies more for emerging (1-10%+).

slides.title: Limitations + alternatives to GDP
slides.body:
**What GDP measures well**: economic activity through markets, output produced, value generated.

**What GDP misses**:
- **Non-market activities**: household production (childcare, cooking, cleaning), volunteer work. Worth ~25% of GDP if priced.
- **Informal economy**: estimated 5-30% of GDP in many countries.
- **Quality + variety improvements**: hedonic adjustments + chain-weighting help but imperfect (smartphone vs 1990s phone — same 'price' but different product).
- **Inequality**: GDP is average; doesn't show distribution.
- **Environmental damage**: oil spill that costs $1B in cleanup ADDS to GDP (counted as production), not subtracted.
- **Depletion of natural capital**: extracting oil counts as positive but doesn't subtract the loss of future stock.
- **Subjective well-being + life satisfaction**.
- **Health, education, leisure** (partial; some included).

**Alternative + supplementary measures**:
- **HDI (Human Development Index)**: UN; combines income + life expectancy + education.
- **GPI (Genuine Progress Indicator)**: adjusts GDP for environment + inequality + non-market.
- **Inclusive Wealth Index**: capital stocks instead of flows.
- **Beyond GDP / Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission 2009**: well-being + sustainability metrics.
- **GDP+ adjustments**: NetGDP (subtract environmental damage); Adjusted Net Savings (subtract resource depletion).
- **OECD Better Life Index**: 11 dimensions.
- **Gallup Well-Being Index**: subjective.
- **Bhutan's Gross National Happiness**.

**Modern uses + critiques**:
- GDP remains workhorse for macroeconomic policy, fiscal/monetary decisions, international comparisons.
- Critics: distorts policy toward growth at expense of other goods.
- Defenders: GDP correlates strongly with most outcomes (health, education, infant mortality); no single replacement does what GDP does.
- Modern practice: GDP + supplementary indicators + sectoral data.

slides.title: Modern challenges: digital + intangible economy
slides.body:
The 21st-century economy is increasingly:
• **Digital**: software, AI, platforms.
• **Intangible**: brand, knowledge, IP, organizational capital, network effects.
• **Services-dominant**: ~80% of US GDP services.
• **Globalized**: complex supply chains; arbitrary attribution to countries.

**GDP measurement challenges**:
1. **Free digital services**: Google search, Facebook, Wikipedia, ChatGPT — high consumer value, $0 market price. GDP misses entirely. Brynjolfsson + colleagues estimate consumer surplus from digital ~$30K/yr per US household.

2. **Cloud computing + 'as-a-service'**: Capex → opex shift; investment may register as consumption.

3. **Quality improvements + hedonic adjustment**: smartphone of 2024 has dozens of features unimaginable in 2000. Statistical agencies use hedonic pricing to capture; imperfect.

4. **Cross-border tax + transfer-pricing**: multinationals shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions; GDP attribution distorted (Ireland's pharma + tech reporting inflates GDP).

5. **Intangible investment**: R&D, software, brand. SNA 2008 includes R&D + software in GDP (was missed); brand + organizational capital still missing.

6. **Climate + nature**: as above, externalities + depletion missing.

**Modernization efforts**:
- **System of National Accounts (SNA)** updates every ~25 years; SNA 2008 added R&D; SNA 2025 (in development) addresses globalization, environment, digital.
- **Beyond GDP** (UN + OECD): well-being + sustainability dashboards.
- **National Accounts of Well-Being**: explicit measures.
- **Stern Review** + Dasgupta Review (2021): environmental + nature accounting.

**Practical reading**: when interpreting GDP statistics, check:
- Real vs nominal.
- Per-capita vs aggregate.
- Growth rate vs level.
- Adjusted for purchasing-power parity (PPP) for cross-country?
- Coverage of informal + digital sectors.

question.question: Compute GDP via the expenditure approach
question.goal: A small economy has: consumption C=$700B, investment I=$200B, government spending G=$300B, exports X=$150B, imports M=$200B. Compute GDP.

steps.prompt: Real GDP if price index = 1.10 vs base year?
steps.reveal: Real GDP = Nominal / (P/P_base) = 1150 / 1.10 ≈ $1045.5B. The economy's real output is ~$1045B in base-year prices; nominal $1150B reflects 10% inflation.

steps.prompt: If population is 25M, what's per-capita real GDP?
steps.reveal: Per-capita real GDP ≈ $1,045B / 25M = $41,820 per person per year. (For reference: US ~$76K; EU avg ~$45K; China ~$13K; India ~$2.5K, 2024 nominal.)

question.question: Drag to the approximate 2023 US nominal GDP (in trillion USD).
question.explanation: 2023 US nominal GDP: ~$27.4T. Other major economies (2023): China $17.7T nominal (~$33T PPP); Germany $4.5T; Japan $4.2T; UK $3.3T; India $3.7T (~$15T PPP); France $3.0T. World total ~$105T. US accounts for ~25% globally. PPP-adjusted China now larger than US.

question.question: Why does an oil spill ADD to GDP rather than subtract from it?
options: GDP measures market transactions: cleanup costs, lawsuits, restoration spending are all market activities contributing to GDP. The destruction of natural capital + ecosystem damage are NOT counted. This is a fundamental limitation of GDP — it measures economic activity, not welfare or wealth. Proposed corrections: Net Domestic Product subtracting capital depreciation; Genuine Progress Indicator adjusting for environmental damage; Inclusive Wealth Index tracking stocks. None has replaced GDP for policy.
question.explanation:
**GDP + environmental damage paradox**:

*The oil-spill example*:
Deepwater Horizon 2010 oil spill cost ~$60B in cleanup, legal settlements, restoration. All counted as positive GDP contributions:
- Cleanup contractors hired (services).
- Lawyers + courts active (services).
- New equipment manufactured (goods).
- Restoration ecology employed (services).

NOT counted:
- ~5M barrels oil released → ecosystem damage.
- Fish + bird + tourism impacts.
- Health effects on humans + animals.
- Loss of natural capital.

Net effect: positive contribution to GDP despite massive welfare loss.

*Why GDP works this way*:
GDP = market value of goods + services produced. Designed to measure economic activity, not welfare. Externalities (positive or negative) generally invisible unless they trigger market transactions.

*Related problems*:

1. **Resource depletion**: extracting oil counts as positive but doesn't subtract loss of future stock. Net Domestic Product (NDP) attempts via depreciation subtraction but underestimates natural capital.

2. **Pollution costs**: only included if cleanup actually occurs.

3. **Climate change**: future damages not in current GDP; carbon pricing partially internalizes.

4. **Biodiversity loss**: nearly invisible to GDP.

*Proposed corrections + alternatives*:

1. **Green GDP** / **Adjusted Net Savings**: subtract depletion + pollution.
2. **Inclusive Wealth Index** (UNEP-IWR): track all capital stocks (produced, human, natural).
3. **Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)**: adjusts GDP for ~30 factors including environment + inequality.
4. **System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA)**: UN framework integrating environment with national accounts.
5. **Natural Capital Accounting**: country-level (UK, Norway, Australia have programs).

*Why GDP remains primary*:

1. **Comparable across time + countries**: ~75 years of consistent methodology.
2. **Correlated with welfare proxies** (life expectancy, education, infant mortality) up to mid-income.
3. **Available + frequent**: quarterly + monthly indicators.
4. **Policy-friendly**: monetary + fiscal policy targeting GDP.

*Criticisms + modern responses*:
- Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission 2009: 'beyond GDP.'
- Dasgupta Review 2021: 'economics of biodiversity.'
- New Zealand 2019: 'Wellbeing Budget.'
- Bhutan: Gross National Happiness since 1972.
- OECD: How's Life? + Better Life Index.
- EU: Beyond GDP + Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) indicators.

*Practical practice*:
Most macroeconomic policy still GDP-targeted. Environmental costs increasingly internalized via carbon pricing, taxes, regulation, ESG disclosure. Trend toward 'dual-account' systems: GDP + supplementary environmental + social accounts.

GDP is a great measure for what it measures — but interpreting it as 'welfare' or 'wealth' is a fundamental category error.

slides.workedSolution: GDP measures market transactions; oil-spill cleanup is market activity (counted positive). Ecosystem damage + natural-capital loss not counted. Fundamental limitation: GDP measures activity, not welfare or wealth. Examples: Deepwater Horizon 2010 cleanup ~$60B added to GDP despite ecosystem destruction. Corrections proposed: Green GDP, NDP, Inclusive Wealth Index, GPI, SEEA framework. None has replaced GDP for policy; GDP remains primary due to consistency + comparability + correlation with welfare proxies. Modern: dual-account systems (GDP + environmental + social accounts).

question.question: Nominal GDP = $1500B; GDP deflator = 125 (2010 base = 100). Real GDP?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why GDP per capita is a useful but imperfect measure of national well-being.
question.rubric: Mentions: GDP per capita: nominal GDP divided by population. Useful: correlated with welfare proxies (life expectancy, education, infant mortality) particularly up to mid-income range; allows cross-country + cross-time comparison; available quarterly. Limitations: averages out inequality (US has higher GDP per capita than EU but worse life expectancy + health); ignores externalities + nature + non-market activity + leisure; quality + variety improvements imperfectly captured; PPP adjustments matter for cross-country (China $13K nominal but $24K PPP). Modern alternatives: HDI (UN; income+life+education), GPI, OECD Better Life Index, Bhutan GNH, Dasgupta Review natural capital. None has displaced GDP for policy; pragmatic: GDP + supplementary indicators + sectoral metrics. Concludes: GDP is useful summary but interpretation requires care; per-capita helps but ignores distribution + quality + externalities; complementary indicators essential for full welfare assessment.
